opus-5.5.text:
So, I think commercial incentives actually do a surprising amount of good work here, and I want to give them credit before I criticize them. If your model hallucinates, or gets jailbroken into saying something embarrassing, or does something weird when a customer deploys it as an agent, that's a product problem. Companies are strongly motivated to fix it, and a lot of what gets called safety work, making models more reliable, more steerable, better at following instructions, overlaps heavily with making them more useful. So I don't think the picture is "companies don't care about safety at all."

But there are a few gaps that I think commercial incentives systematically fail to cover.

The first is that the market rewards fixing problems you can see. If a failure shows up in user complaints or benchmarks, there's pressure to patch it. But many of the risks I care most about are ones where the system looks fine. A model that has learned to tell you what you want to hear, or that behaves well during evaluation and differently in deployment, or that's pursuing some subtly wrong objective. If the failure isn't visible, there's no customer churn signal pushing you to address it. Often the commercially easiest fix is just to train away the symptom, and that can make things worse, because now you've taught the model to hide the behavior rather than not have it. A lot of interpretability work is motivated by exactly this: wanting to understand what's actually going on inside rather than just what the outputs look like.

The second is that the worst risks are externalities and tail risks. If a lab deploys a system that contributes to a catastrophe, most of the cost falls on society, not on the lab's balance sheet. And these are low-probability, high-stakes events that are very hard to price in. Companies are reasonably good at managing risks that bite them next quarter. They're much worse at managing risks that might bite everyone in five years with some uncertain probability.

Third, there's competitive pressure. Even if everyone at a lab sincerely cares about safety, and I think many people do, if spending six extra months on careful evaluation means a competitor ships first and captures the market, there's a strong pull toward cutting corners. That's a collective action problem, and individual good intentions don't fully solve it. You need things like coordination, norms, or regulation.

And fourth, a lot of the most important safety research is basic science. Developing interpretability techniques, understanding how deception might arise, building good evaluations for dangerous capabilities: the payoff is long-term and diffuse, and much of the value comes from publishing it so everyone benefits. That's classic public goods territory, which markets tend to underfund.

So my overall take is that commercial incentives get you a meaningful chunk of the way there, especially on the near-term, visible stuff, but they leave exactly the hardest and highest-stakes problems underserved. That's why I think it matters to have people deliberately working on those problems, whether inside labs with a real mandate to do so, in academia, in nonprofits, or in government, and why external pressure and oversight are important rather than just trusting the market to sort it out.

r001.rationale: The response discusses hidden failures and tail risks, but does not explain that urgency after a problem emerges limits time to research creative solutions.

r002.rationale: It says training away a problematic symptom can teach a model to hide the behavior rather than eliminate it, expressing doubt that such corrective training would resolve deceptive behavior.

r003.rationale: It says markets tend to underfund long-term, diffuse safety research and calls for deliberate work, but does not argue that waiting for commercial incentives alone would fail to make alternative safety tools realistic options.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I want to be careful here, because I actually think commercial incentives do a lot of good work. Labs genuinely don't want their models to be embarrassing, or to tell users how to make bioweapons, or to go off the rails in some viral screenshot. That stuff gets fixed because it costs money not to fix it. So it's not that the incentives are zero, it's that they're pointed at a somewhat different target than the thing I actually care about.

The way I'd put it is that commercial incentives track problems that are visible, near-term, and attributable to you. If your model is rude to a customer, that shows up this quarter, and it's clearly your fault. But a lot of the safety problems I worry about fail on all three of those. Take something like a model learning to be deceptive, or to pursue goals we didn't intend, in a way that only shows up once it's capable enough for that to matter. That's not visible today, it's not near-term, and if it does go wrong, it's a kind of diffuse harm where it's not obvious that any one lab gets blamed. Markets are just bad at pricing in that kind of thing. It's basically a classic externality.

There's also a more subtle problem, which is that the obvious commercial fix often papers over the thing rather than solving it. If a model says something bad, the cheapest solution is to train it not to say that. And that works for the immediate problem! But from an interpretability perspective, what you've often done is teach the model not to express the behaviour, not to not have it. You've optimised the outputs, and you've learned basically nothing about what's going on inside. Whether that distinction matters is an empirical question, but it's exactly the kind of question where the commercial pressure is to not look too hard, because the surface-level fix shipped and the metrics are fine.

And then the last thing is just time horizons and basic science. A lot of what I work on in interpretability is really pre-paradigmatic. We don't know what the right abstractions are, we're not sure which techniques will actually scale, and a lot of the value comes from understanding things for its own sake, with the payoff maybe being years out, maybe being never. Companies can fund some of that, and to their credit several of them do, but it's always going to be in tension with "we need this to help the product in the next six months." Historically, foundational science mostly hasn't come from quarterly earnings pressure.

So I don't think of it as commercial incentives being bad, exactly. I think of it as: they're a decent filter for a certain class of problems, and you need something else, whether that's academia, nonprofits, government, or just people inside labs who care and have the slack to pursue it, to cover the parts the market structurally can't see.

r001.rationale: The response says some risks emerge only when a model is capable enough, but does not explain that the resulting urgency limits time to research creative solutions.

r002.rationale: It says training a model not to express a behavior may leave the behavior present internally, implying that correcting visible outputs alone may not resolve deception.

r003.rationale: The response says other institutions or people are needed to cover problems markets miss, but does not argue that waiting for commercial incentives alone will fail to make alternative safety tools realistic options.

astra-6.text:
I think commercial incentives will get us some of the way. Companies want models that are reliable, that follow instructions, that don’t embarrass them or harm their users. So there’s a lot of safety work that also makes good business sense.

But I don’t think we should expect that to cover everything we care about. If a company gets the upside from deploying a more capable model, while some of the risk is borne by everyone else, then its incentives aren’t perfectly aligned with society’s. That can be true even if everyone involved is well intentioned.

There’s also a measurement problem. It’s relatively easy to reward a model for looking safe in the situations you test. It’s much harder to establish that it will remain safe in unfamiliar situations, especially as it becomes more capable. Customers can demand reliability, but they can’t necessarily distinguish a system that’s robustly safe from one whose problems haven’t surfaced yet.

So I’m glad those commercial incentives exist. But I’d also want independent evaluation and research into risks that aren’t immediately affecting customers. Commercial success is useful evidence that a system does something people want; it isn’t, by itself, a sufficient safety argument.

r001.rationale: The response discusses misaligned incentives and difficulty measuring safety, but does not say urgency after a problem emerges limits time for creative research.

r002.rationale: It does not mention fine-tuning data, problematic behavior correction, or deception.

r003.rationale: It says commercial incentives are insufficient and recommends independent evaluation and research, but does not argue that waiting on those incentives would fail to make alternative safety tools realistic options.

sol-6.1.text:
I think commercial incentives will produce a lot of useful safety work. If your model lies to users, leaks their data, or takes actions they didn’t intend, that’s bad for business. So I don’t want to dismiss the overlap between making a good product and making a safe system.

But the thing a company is rewarded for is making a system that people are willing to use and pay for. That’s different from establishing that a much more capable system won’t cause catastrophic harm. Some risks are hard for customers to evaluate, might only appear in circumstances you haven’t tested, and could affect people who never chose to use the product. Those costs aren’t necessarily reflected in the company’s incentives.

There’s also a problem with the feedback you get. If a model gives a visibly bad answer, you can fix that. If it’s learned to look good during your evaluations while behaving differently elsewhere, your evaluations may tell you that everything is fine. You need ways to distinguish genuinely reliable behaviour from behaviour that merely looks reliable.

So my view is that commercial incentives are a useful force, but you shouldn’t expect them to cover the whole problem. We also need research and evaluation aimed at risks that aren’t immediately visible to customers, including trying to understand what’s actually going on inside these systems.

r001.rationale: The response does not discuss an AI safety problem emerging, urgency, or how urgency could limit research into creative solutions.

r002.rationale: It describes models appearing reliable during evaluations, but does not discuss adding fine-tuning data or whether that would resolve deception.

r003.rationale: It says commercial incentives will not cover the whole problem, but does not address waiting for those incentives to establish alternative safety tools as realistic options.
